bigPicture.note: These are YouTubers' claims, not advice.

agree.title: Where they agree
agree.text: Post-midterm years have been strong for stocks. Their cited stat: about 16% for the S&P over the next 12 months.

views.title: The index fund itself is the risk
Power, crypto and Tesla
views.detail: AI power as the last growth engine.

views.title: Follow government spending
views.detail: Plus a cash cushion and a dollar hedge.

videos.title: The Wealth Transfer Has Officially Started
videos.gist: He says a 2008-style wealth transfer is starting, with money rotating from stocks into crypto, and his Bitcoin-halving model put the bottom around Nov 7, 2026. He buys altcoins, not Bitcoin, and the last 10 minutes sell a $29/month community and a $1,000 non-refundable call for people with $250K+.

points.title: Wealth transfers happen in crashes
points.text: He says after 2008 the bottom half's inflation-adjusted wealth fell 79% vs about 21% for the top 1%, and the assets that bounce back fastest (stocks last time) make the rich richer.

points.title: The rich hold stocks, not real estate
points.text: He cites the top 10% owning 88% of corporate equity and fund holdings in Q2 2026, compared with 44% of real estate.

points.title: 46 companies are moving into crypto
points.text: He says 46 companies drove most of the last wealth creation, and names like Apple, Microsoft, NVIDIA, JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard are now building on or buying crypto.

points.title: Halving makes Bitcoin predictable
points.text: Bitcoin's new supply is cut in half about every four years (next one early 2028), with a 21 million cap. He shows 541, 512 and 514 days from past bottoms to the halving.

points.title: His model's bottom call
points.text: He says the same model put the bottom at Nov 7, 2026. He claims it helped him sell 80% of his crypto in late October, near the top.

points.title: Altcoins over Bitcoin
points.text: He says his study of 500 altcoins found an average 33.3x last cycle vs 8x for Bitcoin, and most altcoin peaks came before the halving.

points.title: His coin filters
points.text: Already regulated as a commodity, far below its all-time high (ideally about 90%), big gains last cycle, backed by the 46 companies, and low liquidity. His final three coins appear on screen; he doesn't say their names out loud.

points.title: Three skills to trade
points.text: Pick coins (fundamental analysis), manage the portfolio instead of buy-and-hope, and read market direction. He claims buy-and-hope gives you above an 84% chance of losing everything.

todo: Treat the Nov 7 bottom call as one creator's model, not a fact
Check any coin's regulation status, liquidity and drawdown yourself before buying
Don't pay for a group or a non-refundable call because a video says the door is closing

stamps.label: Altcoin peaks come before the halving

videos.watch: This is a sales pitch: the last 10+ minutes sell his $29/month Skool community and a $1,000 non-refundable call that requires proof of $250K in liquid crypto, with fake urgency ("shutting the door", 10 days, Black Friday). The 88%/46-company stats, the Nov 7 bottom model, his 80% sell and 127x/$11M claims, and the 500-coin 33x study are his own and not checked here. He also frames it as a message from God. Not advice.

videos.title: AI Must Grow Fast Or The Market Implodes
videos.gist: He says the bond market is flashing crash warnings while stocks sit at all-time highs, and the whole rally rides on AI. If AI revenue doesn't grow fast enough to pay for the data-center build-out, he expects bankruptcies and a big drop.

points.title: Bond yields as a crash warning
points.text: He cites Bank of America's chief strategist pointing to three times bond yields ripped higher right before a crash: Japan 1989, the U.S. 1999 and China 2007. He says the same pattern is showing up now, and in several big economies at once, which leaves fewer safe places to move money.

points.title: Stocks don't agree with bonds
points.text: While bonds signal distress, the stock market is at a fresh all-time high. He says prices assume a huge, fast jump in value that has to arrive before the build-out costs catch up.

points.title: Chip stocks are stretched
points.text: He says the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index is 62% above its 200-day moving average, the widest gap in the index's history.

points.title: Shiller CAPE over 40
points.text: He says it has only crossed 40 twice in about 150 years: 1929 and 1999, both followed by huge crashes. At 40, investors pay $40 for every $1 of average inflation-adjusted earnings (long-run average about 17), and he says studies imply a 10-year S&P return near zero or negative.

points.title: A 1720-style bubble comparison
points.text: He says Bank of America's strategist now compares this to the Mississippi bubble of 1720, not just the dot-com bubble.

points.title: Seven stocks, one bet
points.text: He says the Magnificent Seven are about 30% of the U.S. market, and nearly all the growth rides on AI and its costly infrastructure build-out.

points.title: Build-outs breed bankruptcies
points.text: Railroads in the UK and U.S. and the telecom build-out for the internet all wiped people out when revenue lagged spending. The tech wasn't bad, he says, but early owners went bust and the next owners reaped the gains.

todo: Check how much of your portfolio leans on the Magnificent Seven and AI/chip stocks
Watch bond yields, not just stock prices
Watch whether AI revenue keeps up with data-center spending
Don't make a big move off one short clip; check the numbers yourself first
videos.watch: Short 5-minute clip with no sponsor in it. The bond-yield pattern, the 62% chip gap, the CAPE figures and the Mississippi-bubble comparison are his or his quoted strategist's, not verified here. Crash calls are a prediction, not a promise. Not advice.

videos.title: Stocks, Gold and Bitcoin All Crashed at Once. Here’s What’s Next
videos.gist: Stocks, gold and Bitcoin all fell together in 45 days, but he says company profits didn't crash — a liquidity drain that started in July did. He thinks liquidity is already turning back up, so don't panic-sell the bounce. Zoom out, and watch the Fed and the dollar.

points.title: The same 45-day window
points.text: About $6 trillion came out of U.S. stocks. In that stretch Nvidia fell 48%, Bitcoin 31%, and gold 15%. Monday's bounce was big, but he says they're still way down, and the bounce alone doesn't settle whether this is a crash or a 2020-style setup.

points.title: The headlines don't add up
points.text: Fear shot up, and people are calling it an AI-bubble pop. He says S&P 500 earnings still grew about 33%, the strongest in four years, and Nvidia now trades at about 9 times forward earnings with 75% guidance. When stocks, gold and Bitcoin fall together, he reads that as a liquidity problem, not just a tech story.

points.title: The real cause started in July
points.text: He treats liquidity like a tide: more of it lifts prices, less of it drops them, and it typically leads tech by about 13 weeks. July's drain shows up in October and November. Two huge IPOs (SpaceX, then Anthropic) raised about $156 billion, and Treasury issuance hit about $162 billion in November, all when liquidity was already tight.

points.title: Then came the accelerants
points.text: The Fed had already hiked and then held rates tight in October. Midterms added a short-term hit, especially after talk of curbing data centers. Jensen Huang stepped down, leverage got wiped out (he took calls from people in margin calls), and the dollar ripped higher from Nov 9. That mix, he says, made the drop fast and violent.

points.title: What he thinks comes next
points.text: Like 2020, the drain came first. He says liquidity is already turning back up, on a lag, and markets are starting to price that in over the next couple of months if it continues. Watch the next Fed meeting (hike, hold, or cut) and the dollar. He also says tech valuations have fallen below the March 2020 low even though profits are strong.

points.title: Zoom out before you sell
points.text: Since 2018, Nvidia has had many drawdowns as big as this one, or bigger, and is still up almost 8,000% if you held. The S&P had several 20–35% drops and is up 234%. Bitcoin is more violent (he lists 50–70% drawdowns) but still up about 4,000% on that same view.

points.title: Bitcoin is his liquidity canary
points.text: He puts Bitcoin furthest out on the risk curve, past tech and AI, so it reacts first to global liquidity. He says Bitcoin starting to recover is a sign liquidity is coming back. On-chain, most of the recent selling came from people who bought the top and sold the bottom.

todo: Don't make a sell-or-buy decision off this week's bounce or a headline
Watch the next Fed meeting and whether liquidity keeps rising
Watch the dollar; another spike would pressure stocks, gold and Bitcoin again
If you use margin or leverage, this is the reminder to get off it
Zoom out on any holding that's down hard before you sell it

stamps.label: Why the headlines don't add up
Rates, Huang, leverage and the dollar

videos.watch: He pitches a paid 3-day 'wealth engineering' workshop on January 6–8, 2027. The $6 trillion, earnings, valuation and IPO figures are his. He recorded this after Monday's bounce and even floats that it could be a dead-cat bounce. Not advice, and a midterm-year rally is a pattern, not a promise.

videos.title: When Fear Hits This Level, Stocks Usually Do THIS
videos.gist: After Friday's drop, the S&P is in a correction and the VIX closed at 35.9. Their six-gauge dashboard says this looks like a sharp AI-stock selloff, not 2008 — but the market usually falls a bit more first, and rates are the risk to watch.

points.title: How far it has fallen
points.text: The S&P peaked on Oct 6 and is 11.6% below that, 33 trading days later. Friday: S&P down 3.7%, Nasdaq 5.3%, chips almost 11%. The Nasdaq 100 is down 19.8%, a hair from a bear market. Semiconductors are down 42% since June. Only consumer staples rose among the 11 S&P sectors.

points.title: Gauges 1 and 2: panic in the options market
points.text: The VIX closed at 35.9, the highest close since the April 2025 tariff crash. Short-term protection is more expensive than 3-month protection (40.7 vs 30.9), which is rare and usually shows up deep in a selloff. Individual investors are 51% bearish, versus a long-run average of about 31%.

points.title: Gauge 3: the selling is narrow
points.text: About a quarter of S&P stocks actually rose on Friday. The damage is in chips and AI, led by Nvidia: Jensen Huang resigned on Nov 12, then the SEC news hit, and the stock fell about 14% on Friday, roughly 47% below its October high. Revenue still beat, and its outlook already assumes no China data-center chip sales.

points.title: Gauges 4 and 5: credit and earnings look calm
points.text: Junk bond spreads are 3.52 points, the high for this year, but well under the 4.61 of April 2025. They've widened only 0.17 of a point, not the 1–2 points seen before 2001 and 2008. S&P earnings grew 32.9% last quarter, forecasts are still being raised, and the index is about 16.5 times next year's earnings, below its 10-year average of 19.1.

points.title: The catch on earnings: AI spending
points.text: Alphabet, Meta and Amazon are spending more than their operating cash (Amazon is about $42B in the red over 12 months). Only Microsoft still covers its bill. Cloud revenue is still growing fast. If that spending stops paying off, they say this gauge breaks first, when earnings forecasts get cut.

points.title: Gauge 6: rates are stressed
points.text: The Fed already hiked in September to 3.75–4%, inflation is 3.7%, and it meets again on Dec 9. After Friday the market still priced about a 92% chance of another hike, with rates peaking around 4.5%. The 10-year yield is 4.91%, down from 5.31% in early October. Oil is still near $90, and a new Congress plus a Jan 10 trade-truce deadline add political risk. Higher rates hit every stock, not just AI.

points.title: What usually happens after a VIX close above 35
points.text: Since 1990 they found 17 similar first spikes. Six months later the S&P was higher 15 times; a year later, 14 times, with a median gain of 21.6% versus 11.9% in an average year. That is not a bottom call. After those days the S&P usually fell more first (median about 6%). The three misses were 2001, 2008 and March 2022.

points.title: Their read, and what would change it
points.text: This looks more like a sharp correction in AI stocks than the start of 2008: fear is in options, not in credit or earnings. The warning light that matches a bad case is rates (like 2022). Watch for junk spreads above about 4.5 points, earnings forecasts getting cut, or a Dec 9 hike plus a 10-year yield back above 5.25%.

todo: Don't treat a high VIX as a buy-the-bottom signal; in their past cases the S&P usually fell about 6% more first
Watch junk bond spreads; a move above about 4.5 points would mean lenders are backing off
Watch whether analysts start cutting earnings forecasts, especially if AI spending stops paying off
Mark the calendar: Dec 1 Huang's testimony, Dec 9 Fed, Dec 10 inflation report, Jan 10 trade truce
videos.watch: A small channel with its own six-gauge dashboard, not advice. They used 17 cases and picked 35 as a round VIX cutoff; returns are price-only, no dividends. Nvidia and SEC details are from news reports they cite. The next few dates can change the picture fast.

videos.title: The Government is DESPERATE for You to Start This Business
videos.gist: The government already pays small businesses million-dollar contracts for ordinary work. He says the winners research early on SAM.gov and USAspending.gov. They don't wait for an RFP and fire off proposals.

points.title: Five real small-business awards
points.text: Tree maintenance ($1.76M), fire alarm upgrades ($690K, about $510M a year in spend), kosher/halal food for federal prisons ($1M), hospital wandering-protection alarms (about $150M a year), and an $18M airplane hangar repair.

points.title: Don't chase RFPs
points.text: Writing proposals on SAM.gov is the last step. He says companies that only do that rarely win.

points.title: Research past awards first
points.text: On USAspending.gov, look up your NAICS or keywords. See yearly spend, which agencies buy, which states get the work, and who already wins.

points.title: Answer Sources Sought early
points.text: These are questions, not bids. Send your capability statement and recommendations before the solicitation comes out. If you can't do the whole job, look for a teammate or a subcontract.

points.title: Check procurement forecasts
points.text: Acquisition.gov and the Navy long-range forecast list upcoming work, dollar ranges, incumbents, a contracting contact, and the target quarter. Funding can still change.

points.title: For Penguin Air
points.text: You don't have to learn all of government contracting. Just how the government buys HVAC and plumbing. Start with facilities and mechanical work near bases and federal buildings in the Carolinas.

todo: Search USAspending.gov for HVAC, plumbing and facilities maintenance spend near NC
On SAM.gov, filter Sources Sought for mechanical, HVAC and plumbing work
Note bonding, licenses, past performance and base-access requirements before you reply
Check Acquisition.gov forecasts (and nearby DoD ones) for upcoming facilities jobs
If a Sources Sought is bigger than you can do alone, find a teammate or offer to subcontract
videos.watch: This is also a pitch for his paid GovClose program. The dollar figures are his read of public data and they change. No contract is guaranteed.

videos.title: Build Your Own AI Chief of Staff in 6 Steps
videos.gist: You don't need your own AI model. Connect the right pieces and you get an assistant that knows your business and does tasks for you.

points.title: 1. Give it a home
points.text: A computer or cloud server that runs 24/7. He prefers the cloud.

points.title: 2. Install an agentic harness
points.text: Tools so it can click, type and run tasks. He uses Hermes.

points.title: 3. Choose its AI brain
points.text: Claude, ChatGPT or an open-source model.

points.title: 4. Teach it who you are
points.text: Let it interview you about your business, offers, clients and goals.

points.title: 5. Give it a persistent memory
points.text: A second brain tied to your files, contacts and key info.

points.title: 6. Add skills
points.text: Explain a job once. It remembers and repeats it every day.

todo: Pick a home that runs 24/7 (a cloud server is easiest)
Install an agent harness that can click, type and run tasks
Choose the AI model that powers it
Let it interview you about your business, offers, clients and goals
Connect its memory to your files, contacts and key info
Teach it one job at a time as a saved skill
videos.watch: Lead-magnet reel: 'comment JARVIS' gets you his guide. 'One weekend' is his claim. Hermes is his pick, not a tested comparison. Be careful what files and accounts you connect.

videos.title: A Beginner Homelab You Can Start Today
videos.gist: You can start a home server on a laptop you already have, run your own Netflix and Google Drive with Docker, and reach it from your phone with Tailscale so you don't open your home to the internet.

points.title: 1. Use an old laptop
points.text: Start with one you already have. 256 GB of storage is enough to begin. Use 500 GB or more if you want movies on it.

points.title: 2. Keep the OS, or switch to Ubuntu Server
points.text: Windows is fine to start. Or install Ubuntu Server, a free operating system made for running servers.

points.title: 3. Install Docker
points.text: It's free. It runs each app in its own box, so adding an app takes one command instead of a whole project.

points.title: 4. Add the apps you actually want
points.text: Jellyfin works like your own Netflix for movies you already have. Nextcloud works like your own Google Drive for files.

points.title: 5. Reach it from your phone with Tailscale
points.text: Tailscale is a free app that links your devices on a private network. You can use the server from anywhere without opening your home to the internet.

points.title: 6. Upgrade only when you outgrow it
points.text: When the laptop isn't enough, move to a Raspberry Pi (it uses very little power), then a mini PC or a full server.

points.title: Tools
points.text: An old laptop, Docker, Jellyfin, Nextcloud, and Tailscale. Optional later: Ubuntu Server, a Raspberry Pi, a mini PC, or a rack server.

points.title: Safety notes
points.text: Don't open ports on your home router to the internet — that's why he uses Tailscale. Keep the laptop updated, and back up anything you put in Nextcloud. Jellyfin is only for media you have the right to store.

todo: Pick an old laptop with at least 256 GB (500 GB or more if you want movies on it)
Keep Windows, or install Ubuntu Server if you want a dedicated machine
Install Docker
Add Jellyfin and/or Nextcloud
Install Tailscale on the laptop and your phone — don't open ports to the internet
When the laptop isn't enough, move to a Raspberry Pi, then a mini PC or a server
videos.watch: Short beginner reel, and 'cancel your subscriptions' is his hook. A home server still needs updates and backups. Use Tailscale like he shows; don't open your home to the internet.

videos.title: How to Run Your Own Private AI
videos.gist: You can run AI on hardware you control so files never go to OpenAI or Anthropic. He shows a solo Mac setup and a team server, then how to chat with your documents and lock it down.

points.title: 1. Pick a model with the memory rule
points.text: Size in billions × about 0.6 = GB needed, then leave room for the chat and other apps. A 9B model needs about 7 GB (fine on a 16 GB Mac). A ~30B model needs about 20 GB (32–64 GB RAM). 128 GB can run OpenAI's GPT-OSS 120B. His picks: Qwen 3 9B, then a larger Qwen 3 mixture-of-experts that only uses about 3B per word.

points.title: 2. Solo path: your own Mac (most private)
points.text: Easiest: LM Studio. No terminal. Search a model, download it, load it, drag in a PDF and ask. Full setup: Ollama runs the model (install from ollama.com), Open WebUI is the chat screen (Docker Desktop, then open localhost:3000). Raise Ollama's context length to 16K, and turn Cloud off so models don't run on their servers.

points.title: 3. Team path: a private Ubuntu server
points.text: Plain Ubuntu, no ready-made template. Official install scripts for Ollama, Docker, Open WebUI and Docling. Example he used: Hostinger KVM, 8 cores and 32 GB, about $26/month on the 2-year promo and about $50 at renewal. No graphics card, so it's slow (a few words a second). If 32 GB struggles, drop to the 9B model.

points.title: 4. Put it on your domain with Caddy
points.text: One DNS record, one Caddy install, HTTPS that renews itself. Create the first account right away — it becomes the admin. On a CPU box, turn thinking mode off or it adds a lot of waiting. No domain? Use Tailscale instead.

points.title: 5. Chat with company documents (RAG)
points.text: In Open WebUI, fix document settings before you upload anything (changing them later means reprocessing). Set the embedding model, turn on hybrid search so names and invoice numbers match, and point scanned PDFs at Docling or uploads fail. Create a Knowledge collection, then type # in a chat and pick it. Answers show citations to the exact paragraph.

points.title: 6. Lock it down, in this order
points.text: 2FA on the hosting account. SSH keys, then password login off. Firewall with only ports 22, 80 and 443 open. Never open Ollama's port 11434 — it has no password. Keep software updated. Turn new sign-ups off and add people yourself. Open WebUI has no built-in 2FA, so use Google or Microsoft login, or put it on Tailscale so only your team can see it. Snapshot before every update.

points.title: 7. The honest limits
points.text: A rented server is still someone else's computer. Hostinger's terms say it's not a HIPAA or payment-card environment, so no patient data and no card numbers. Running it yourself doesn't make you compliant — it makes you responsible. Most private option: a machine in your own office with disk encryption on.

points.title: 8. Add n8n for real work
points.text: Install n8n on the same server with one more Docker command and its own Caddy address. Don't use the host's n8n template — a new template can wipe the server. Point n8n at your Ollama model. Then you can pull dates out of a contract uploaded through a form, sort tickets and draft replies, or write a Monday report, and the AI never leaves the server.

points.title: Tools and cost
points.text: LM Studio or Ollama, Docker, Open WebUI, Docling, Caddy, optional Tailscale and n8n. A server is about $26–$50 a month. A 64 GB Mac Mini is a one-time cost, a little under $3,000. A rented graphics card full-time is about $250–$500 a month. Hourly GPU boxes (from about 40 cents/hour) have no backups and get deleted if credit hits zero — don't keep the company brain there.

points.title: Common mistakes
points.text: Don't leave Ollama open to the internet. Researchers found about 17,500 exposed servers; a flaw called Bleeding Llama could leak conversations. Don't upload files before fixing document settings. Delete old policy versions or it will quote the wrong one. Spreadsheets are a trap: search only pulls a few rows, so keep Excel for totals.

todo: Decide solo (your own Mac, most private) vs a team server
If solo: install LM Studio, pick a model that fits your RAM, and drag in a test PDF
If a server: use plain Ubuntu and official install commands — don't use a host template that can wipe the box
In Open WebUI, set embedding, hybrid search and Docling before you upload any files
Lock it down: 2FA, SSH keys, firewall on 22/80/443 only, never open port 11434, turn sign-ups off
Keep customer or card data off a rented VPS. If it has to stay private, use a machine in the office with disk encryption
videos.watch: He also pitches his paid community; exact commands are in a free blog post linked from his profile. A rented VPS is still someone else's computer, and Hostinger says it's not a HIPAA or card-data setup. Captions were messy on some model names (Qwen 3 9B and a larger Qwen 3 mixture-of-experts).

videos.title: A Once In A 100 Year Investment Opportunity Just Started
videos.gist: The S&P looks calm, but most stocks are already in a bear market. He thinks three things lining up make this a rare setup.

points.title: Hidden bear market
points.text: He says about 60% of US stocks are down 20%+ from their highs.

points.title: AI and chips hit hardest
points.text: His figure: 9 in 10 down 20%+, 4 in 10 lost half.

points.title: Index = about 8 stocks
points.text: A few giant tech names carry the S&P, so an index fund is one big bet.

points.title: AI spending digest
points.text: Weak players wash out, like railways and the internet, then survivors win.

points.title: Midterms clear the fog
points.text: He cites S&P gains averaging 16% in the 12 months after midterms.

points.title: Money taps reopening
points.text: M2 growing fastest in about 4 years. The Fed is buying again.

points.title: Market isn't the economy
points.text: 2020: 15% unemployment, record highs. 2022: low unemployment, market fell 19%.

todo: Look at what your index fund actually holds
Judge a business on 3 questions: sales growing, profits growing, good return on what it owns
Follow where money is flowing instead of marrying one stock

videos.watch: A funnel for his free training and paid Winston app. The percentages are his, not checked. 'Never once in 50 years' overstates the data.

videos.title: Stop Guessing What to Sell. Start Following a Roadmap.
videos.gist: He shows a roofer ranking in Google mainly because of an exact-match domain name, and says a local business should run 10 to 20 vertical-plus-location microsites instead of one website. That's also a pitch for his paid SEO academy, so treat the tactic carefully.

points.title: 1. Search the way a customer would
points.text: Go to Google and type a trade plus a place, like 'roofers in Alabama.' He focuses on local businesses.

points.title: 2. Don't only chase the map pack
points.text: The map results, he says, are hard to crack because they lean on Google reviews. Keep scrolling into the regular blue links.

points.title: 3. Look at the domain name
points.text: He zooms in on a site like RoofingAlabama LLC ranking in the top five and says the name of the website is why it's there. It can be that simple, in his view.

points.title: 4. Build vertical-plus-location microsites
points.text: If he were going after roofing in Alabama, he would register something like roofersalabama.com, then also city sites for Huntsville, Birmingham, Montgomery, Mobile, and so on. He asks: why have just one website?

points.title: 5. He would run 10 to 20 sites for one business
points.text: Sometimes under a DBA ('doing business as'). He claims one laser-targeted microsite can outrank a competitor's entire domain, and that this works best for local businesses, and can also work for e-commerce and professional services.

points.title: What this is really selling
points.text: The Facebook post is for a paid Skool community, AI SEO: Rank Expand Academy — a day-by-day roadmap, courses on local SEO, microsites and n8n, plus live coaching. The roofing site, he says, is not his.

todo: Don't buy a stack of domains off a 2-minute ad
If you want more local Google leads, start with one strong site, your Google Business Profile, and reviews
If the microsite idea still sounds useful, have a marketing pro review it first — a bunch of thin location sites can hurt more than they help
videos.watch: This is a Facebook ad for a paid Skool community. 'One microsite can outrank a whole domain' and '10 to 20 websites for one business' are his claims. Google can treat networks of thin location sites as spam. The example roofer site is one he says he does not own.

videos.title: How to Defer Income Forever
videos.gist: He says you can defer most of your business income forever by selling 95% of your LLC to a special irrevocable trust. A regular living trust will not do it, and he wants you to comment CPA for a free look. Treat this as a pitch, not a plan.

points.title: 1. Set up a very specific kind of trust
points.text: He says it must be a non-grantor, irrevocable, discretionary, complex, spendthrift trust. A standard family or living trust, he says, will not qualify for the deferral.

points.title: 2. Sell 95% of your LLC to that trust
points.text: Do this as a non-officer, he says, and only if the business is an LLC — not a C-corp or S-corp. The idea is the trust owns the majority while you still run day-to-day operations.

points.title: 3. Run income through the LLC, then issue a K-1 to the trust
points.text: Because the trust owns 95%, he claims 95% of the income is deferred inside the trust and can stay deferred forever.

points.title: What he promises
points.text: He says this legally cuts your tax bill by six or seven figures every year. Comment CPA and his page will do a free assessment of you and your business structure.

todo: Do not change Penguin Air's ownership or tax setup from a 60-second reel
If you want a real read, send the video to your own CPA and ask whether any of it applies
Don't comment CPA on the ad or share financials with this page
videos.watch: Lead-magnet reel: 'comment CPA' gets his free assessment. 'Defer income forever' and 'six or seven figures every year' are his claims, not verified. Selling most of your company to a trust you still control is something the IRS looks at closely. Do not set this up from a reel.

videos.title: Should You Build a Homelab?
videos.gist: A homelab is just a computer at home that runs your own apps so you can drop some subscriptions. Start with an old laptop or mini PC, run things like Nextcloud, Jellyfin or Plex, Pi-hole, and Tailscale, and expect a learning curve.

points.title: What a homelab is
points.text: Your own setup at home where you store data, run apps, or experiment with tech. He built one because he got tired of paying for subscriptions he could host himself.

points.title: What you can run
points.text: Nextcloud as your own Google Drive. Jellyfin or Plex as your own Netflix for movies and shows you already have. Pi-hole to block ads on every device on your home network.

points.title: Privacy, control, and access from anywhere
points.text: The big benefit, he says, is you keep the data and you control the setup. Tailscale makes a private network so you can reach the homelab from anywhere.

points.title: You don't need expensive hardware
points.text: The apps he names are free. You can start with an old laptop or a mini PC. There's a learning curve, and he says half the fun is building it the way you want.

todo: If this sounds useful, start with an old laptop or mini PC, not a fancy NAS
Pick one app first (Nextcloud, Jellyfin or Plex, or Pi-hole) instead of all at once
Use Tailscale to reach it from outside the house — don't open your home to the internet
For the step-by-step setup, see the Nov 12 'Beginner Homelab' video already in this library
videos.watch: Short explainer, not a setup guide. 'Cancel your subscriptions' is the hook. The apps are free, but you still need updates and backups, and Jellyfin or Plex is only for media you have the right to store. He asks you to comment if you want a fuller guide.

videos.title: Get Unstuck and Get More Done: 9 Principles
videos.gist: Being stuck is a clarity problem, not laziness. Get clear, calm down, then take the next small step.

points.title: Clarity, not laziness
points.text: Not acting means you lost sight of what, how or why.

points.title: What game am I playing?
points.text: Tie each dull task to your bigger vision.

points.title: Find the fear
points.text: Ask: what am I afraid of that makes this hard?

points.title: Morning brain dump
points.text: 3 columns: negative belief, its opposite, evidence it's true.

points.title: The next 10 feet
points.text: Act on the clarity you have. Confidence comes after.

points.title: No escape hatch
points.text: Find a reason big enough that not acting isn't an option.

points.title: Recommit, don't beat yourself up
points.text: See what led to the slip, then recommit for 24 hours.

points.title: Calm before you push
points.text: Action from stress makes more stress. Shift your state first.

points.title: Journal by hand
points.text: 10–15 minutes: thank, ask for what you want, ask for others.

todo: Make a sheet with 3 columns
Column 1: every negative belief you woke up with
Column 2: the exact opposite, written as a new decision
Column 3: evidence the new decision is true (ask 3 times)
Do 2–4 beliefs a morning, for about 30 days
videos.watch: Built from 7 podcast episodes. 3 were the closest match to the YouTube titles.

videos.title: Sales Objection Replies (Nick Ayala Shorts)
videos.gist: Whoever is explaining is losing. Agree, ask one question, then stop talking.

points.title: “Too expensive” / lowball
points.text: Repeat their number slowly and go quiet. Then: “Help me understand how you got to that.”

points.title: Discount request
points.text: “I can work with you on price. Which part of the work should we take out?”

points.title: “Competitor is cheaper”
points.text: “They might be. Can I ask what's included in their number?”

points.title: “No budget right now”
points.text: “If budget wasn't an issue, would this be a yes?” Then wait.

points.title: “Send me a proposal”
points.text: “Before I write it, what needs to be in there for this to be a yes?”

points.title: “Run it by my partner”
points.text: “What do you think they'll ask you?” Then offer to join that call.

points.title: “We went with someone else”
points.text: “What did they do that I didn't?” and “Can I check back in 90 days?”

todo: Write the key lines down before sales calls
Rehearse them out loud
Run the role-plays in the Notion playbook
After each line, stop talking and let them answer
